analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "I guess. Oh, maybe not. >> [laughter] >> No, thank you. >> K. Good morning everybody. Hello and welcome to the ITF new participant program. Um I'll introduce myself in a moment. Um but you are here in case you're in the wrong room which can happen at ITF meetings. You are here for the new participant program and this is session one of a session seven session program that will take place all day. And this session one is the introduction um the welcome to the ITF um uh all of the tips and tricks about things the gossip that sort of stuff. Okay, this is the best session of the day. So I am uh Jay Daly. I'm the ITF executive director. Um and I've been in this job since about 2019. Um and I'm an internet person. I started using the internet around about 1986 1987. Um and then worked for a long time in the domain name industry. Did a little bit in the IETF and now um the executive director of the ITF. Um I am um uh going to be introducing well introduce my colleague Michelle who you have had um many many emails from over the period of time introducing you and helping you to things. Michelle will be running the session throughout the day. Um and if you have any questions or anything about things ask either Michelle or I about things. Okay. So um what you can expect from today. So the ITF is a big organization um and it's complex and it's broad in scope. Lots of things going on. Um it's a mature organization. It's built up over 40 years. This is the 40th anniversary of the ITF. Um and so it has detailed practices and rules. And all of these things put together can be quite a high barrier of entry for new participants. And so the we've introduced this program to help try to teach you the important things about the ITF because understanding what do I need to know now, what do I not need to know now is is complicated. Um so that you can become a productive and effective ITF participant and to reduce the chances of you giving up. We have data that we know from people that they start with the ITF, they find it far too difficult and they walk away quite soon. So we try to avoid that by you know inducting you through this process so that you understand where things are going. Um um we also aim to build a cohort of new participants. So we have this event where you can talk to each other. We have the um the quick connections later today and we have the dinner later in the week for you to meet each other and talk and build a cohort you know as you go through the ITF. Um we also aim to provide a head start in meeting people. There are um lots of people in leadership within the ITF. Um there are probably 200 or something or more. Um when you take all of the chairs and the various other people together um and they rotate regularly as well. So getting to you know recognize faces and know who people are is useful and helpful for you. So we aim to do that as well. So um and then finally we want to give you an indication of where the the hot topics are, what's being spoken about, what isn't being spoken about. Um so that's the plan. I give this session um as the the staff member who gives this but the rest of the sessions uh apart from one most of the rest of them are given by um community members uh the same as you who've just been doing this for a long time and who we think can reasonably communicate well you know. Um so you'll hopefully learn a lot from the session as you go through it. One other thing because this is such a complex organization and this is such a complex day of events that we we put together sessions to teach you. We we understand that many people need to do this in two bites. So they might come to you know half of it this time round and then for their next meeting come to the other half. No that's fine. That's understood. You you know it takes a while to learn all of these things. So, first things first, just to make sure we're all clear, we need to talk about Mico. Um, because all of your participation relies on Mico. That's a MCO screen over there. This is Mico. Everything is controlled by um Mico. So, it is our um it's our custom tool for remote participation and it's what we use for tracking attendance and for identification. we the reasons why we talk about that later why we need to know who's in certain sessions largely related to intellectual property um considerations and things all sessions are linked off the I the data tracker agenda page um there is a QR code in every session that's the QR code here which you can scan on your phone and which will open up the the meco um uh web tool for you to be able to participate um and we have a little guide to explain to you how to use it and I think Michelle has sent stuff out in advance. So many of you may be familiar with this. Just some little things for you to know straight away. So just get a quick understanding of the features. There are the normal things that you might expect. You can mute and unmute your microphone, turn on off your video. Um then there's joining and exiting the queue with a hand raise button. Those things are normal. Um then we have the chat. Now that's slightly different in that you can use me to go for the chat but this talks to a backend um server of a chat system called Zulip and you can also just use a Zulip client directly to talk to that server and engage as well. [snorts] Then we have the show of hands tool. Um it's not a voting tool. We will be explained later. We don't do voting in the ITF but sometimes this is used or regularly this is used to take the temperature of the room to understand where people are roughly on something. Then we have the the map showing you you know what's happening at the event and um the note takingaking bit. People will talk about the note-taking later, but taking notes during a session is a good way for some newcomers to ensure that they concentrate throughout the session. Um, help them learn what's going on and help them learn to contribute and, you know, um, get start in a session. And then we have the transcription that you can see there. Uh, we have, I think, four rooms that are human transcribed and then the rest of the rooms are AI AI AI transcribed. We've been doing that for um some time now. Um and uh so so that's effectively meter code for you to be able to use to um go forward. Right. So about the ITF then so the ITF essentially is a standards development organization. So its job is to for people to come together to agree on standards and publish those standards and other people to choose whether or not they wish to use those standards. Most importantly, it has no formal membership. Anybody can participate. You can just join an email and participate. Um, people participate as individuals, not as representatives of their employers. Now, what that means is that you have no formal standing by by your employer. You know, because we have no formal membership, your employer cannot buy, you know, a role for anybody in this organization. Now that's very different from many other standards development organizations where employers will buy a seat on the executive committee or a voting seat or something for other people. We don't have that at all. So if you I mean people do say my employer is interested in this and talk about their employer that's perfectly understood. We're not saying you shouldn't do that but you know it doesn't bring any particular authority there. Um our standards here are driven by market-based adoption. You know we as as you will find many people will tell you we are not the internet police. We cannot say to people you must use this standard. You know it is up to the implementers to decide whether or not they wish to use one of our standards. And if we find ourselves writing standards that are not implemented then that's a clear signal we are looking in the wrong direction and need to be doing something else. We are bottomup community controlled. So while I am the executive director, my job is largely to follow policies that have been designed by the community and written down as RFC's. Um it is I I do not come into any of the technical sessions and influence those sessions by you know or have any control over those sessions at all. Um none of the staff do in that way. we that and again that is quite different from other SDOS's where you may well have a staff member who is working with the rest of the community on actively writing the standards that just doesn't happen we don't do that um so everything is controlled by the community here um and everything that you will see has been built by the community and we have a the one of the last sessions of the day is talking about the power of community and how the community has built everything most decisions are made by rough consensus, not by voting. The one the few ones that are made by voting are made within specific leadership groups or groups that are appointed that have rules that say they will use voting such as the nominating committee when it is deciding whether or not to appoint somebody to a role that will do voting. So um and we will have a a long explanation about what rough consensus means later on as well. There is no formal role for governments in the ITF although governments do send people. So we are a multistakeholder model. There are different multistakeholder models. So if you take I can for example the internet corporation for assigned names and numbers a separate multistakeholder body that has um a role for government a role for civil society a role for the technical community and those things we don't work that way. We work in a way where anybody can participate equally in that regard. Um and then the final thing you may have noticed outside here there are no sales booths, no salespeople, um no salesreated activity. The the people that come to the meetings are the people that participate in the meetings [clears throat] whether they are um whether they are engineers, whether they are policy people, whatever they come to participate not to do a meta participation of sales or anything else. Okay. So, at any point if you wish to ask a question, go into me echo, press the show hands thing. Michelle will spot it and then you'll be able to come up to the microphone, you know, and ask a question. Okay. Um, if it if you're struggling with that, just come up to the microphone. Um, that this session's okay with that. Later sessions, you'll probably find people ask you to ensure you do that. So, this is the mission of the ITF. Not the most inspiring mission but technically accurate. So it is intended to make the internet work better by producing good documents that pe that work that people use and choose to adopt. So a brief history of the ITF. Um so the ITF itself was formed in 1986 um by what was then called the internet activities board as an engineering activity. It is the internet engineering task force. Um the first ITF meeting was attended by 21 US federal government funded researchers and a number of them still participate. You'll still see um uh number of them around here. Okay. Um so at least three or four of them I think are possibly here at this time. Uh and if we can get some of them in to say hello, we will do that as well. Certainly for the quick connections. I think later today we tried to get one or two along as well. Not sure. Maybe not this time. Right. Um the ITF initially met three time four times a year. Now it met three times a year and it's always open to the public. The RFC series which the IETF now controls um started before the IETF started with RFC1 published in 1969 by Steve Crocker of UCLA um to organize the working notes of the new ARPANET research program and it's now actually gone over RFC 10,000 rather than approaching RFC 10,000 and Steve Crocker is still a participant in the ITF. Okay. Um the FTP uh one of the early standards of the IATF um or or of the RFC series was defined in early RFC's and RFC's became available via FTP and was therefore the first online publication series itself because you could get it through its own protocol which is lovely. Um and for 28 years it was managed and edited by the internet pioneer John Postell. It's moved on significantly since then, but his influence still stands in many ways. So, I'm going to talk now about the other participants in the ITF, and I'm going to be basing this on data from our annual survey. Every year, we send a survey round to every um address subscribed to one of our mailing lists, which is about 50,000. And we know that of those 50,000 about 7,000 people are active at any one time uh inactive in any one year. Um and we get generally somewhere in the region of um uh 1,700 to 2,000 people reply to our uh survey that we send out and we just published this last week. So we first thing we do is we ask people to categorize themselves as to what kind of participant they are. Um, are they a regular participant? That's straightforward. Are they occasional? Do they occasionally send something to an ITF list? Are they a reader only? Somebody who just reads ITF lists but really doesn't engage. Are they a monitor? Somebody who doesn't who who gets lifts feeds but doesn't really look at it unless they sort of feel that there's something they need to look at. You know, um, there are many senior managers and organizations who do that. you know they have a copy of the list in case anything happens but they don't read it all the time and then we ask there there are a number of people who cease to be participants in the ITF and then new participants people who many of you haven't yet worked out which of the other categories you fit into um so uh as you can see we are skewed here towards the readers and monitors when it comes to the um uh the participants who responded to this survey. So this is while this is useful um the when you read the surve you need to read the survey itself to see what people think broken down by these categories. I can't go into that detail itself now. So this is the breakdown by region. Um as you can see Europe and North America um dominate and have done for quite some time. Asia growing slightly um and certain areas such as Oceanania where I'm from you know are over represented um represented compared to say Africa which is significantly under represented. This is you know voluntary adoption and a voluntary participation but there are obviously barriers to entry that we will talk about um that leads to this breakdown by region. Then we have the breakdown by age and breakdown by gender. So as you can see this is an older organization. The median is somewhere in the 45 to 54 range for people um and there are still people you know significant number of people well over that participating. So over the age of 55 we still have a third or more of participants um participating. Now, gender is the the the the bad story about the IATF here. We have um less than 10% of our participants are women. This is changing considerably particularly with new participants. The demographic among new participants is um approximately 25 to 30% I believe of of new participants are women. um we we don't have any good figures to benchmark this against other than you know normal um society. Um we've looked at um software development where people have done a lot of work on um gender benchmarking that's about 25 30%. But where in our area which is largely engineering we don't have any good benchmarking figures to understand that but this is still something that is changing and is growing over a period of time. [snorts] Then we also ask people about their type of employment and the sector that they work in. And as you can see most of the people here are employees. Um then we have people who um are business owners and generally those are small business owners. Um many of them are consultants or people who used to work for something and now have run their own smaller business. um uh independent contractors and through to um students and others. But to be clear um from looking at the bottom one as you can see while business is top um academia and research comes next. Um so when you look at sector as you can see then we still have healthy participation from civil society and not for profofits and from government as well as from uh business and academia research.
